title: Antharchy storage: EFS for /org on AWS hosts
description:
## Outcome 2026-09-07 — measured out; storage work stops here

**Read this before anything else in this issue. Most decisions below are struck through.**

The campaign under `chatticus-e9ddec` measured this initiative down to almost nothing, and that is the result rather than a failure of it.

| Decision | Fate |
|---|---|
| D1 EFS is the single store | **Narrowed** to `/org` only, "if ever built" — `3d5357`: 23–54x mutating, ~10x read-only warm, in-VPC |
| D2 Local hosts mount EFS over a tunnel | **Superseded** — `9af381`: 1650x at WAN; host class dropped |
| D3 No lease, no snapshot protocol | **Refuted** — the hot tree stays on host disk, so publish/hydrate is permanent |
| D4 Host scratch is not a store | Survives |
| D5 WAN latency handled with stock Linux | **Refuted** — measured |
| D6 Tunnel health is worker health | **Moot** — no tunnel |
| D6a Files versus objects | **Survives, and is the design** |
| D7 Connectivity is a requirement | **Moot** — no tunnel |
| D8 Accelerated batch | Survives, untouched |

**What the shipping design is:** `/workspace` on host-local disk with S3 snapshots for relocate and failover; objects (artifacts, datasets, weights, screenshots) in S3; `/org` on EFS only if a shared read-mostly tree is ever wanted. That is the data-shape split this initiative originally rejected, reinstated by measurement.

**What the campaign bought, in about three days:** it prevented writing `/workspace` EFS CDK, a WireGuard peer, a stopped-when-idle EC2 tunnel endpoint, and an out-of-VPC mount path — and it prevented deleting a working snapshot protocol on D3's authority. The largest single return is that **the architecture already in `develop` was right**, which was not knowable before it was measured.

**Do not reopen without new evidence.** Specifically: do not put `/workspace` on EFS, do not build a tunnel, do not stretch turn timeouts for long jobs, and do not delete the lease or snapshot protocol.

**Still live, and not storage:** accelerated batch (D8) needs a manifold job kind, which needs routines; `chatticus-3c6df9` keeps worker-dials-out for EC2 Antharchy.

---

## Challenge type

This initiative is an **architectural design challenge**. It is discovery-only: no epics, stories, or tasks are attached yet, and nothing here authorizes implementation.

**Status: design conversation concluded 2026-09-03.** This description records the conclusions of that conversation, replacing the earlier draft (which proposed EFS-primary-plus-S3-bridge with a Tailscale connectivity layer). The reasoning that produced each conclusion is preserved below, including the arguments that were tried and rejected, so the decisions can be re-examined rather than re-litigated.

## Context: the three-piece decomposition

Chatticus is decomposing the original "bot" concept (agent + computer + filesystem) into three separate pieces:

1. **The AI agent** — conversation turns, message history, tool use. Owns no compute and no storage.
2. **The compute manifold** — routes declared work kinds to host classes. See `docs/COMPUTER_MANIFOLD.md`.
3. **Storage** — where files live and how every host class reaches them. **This initiative.**

Initiative `chatticus-3c6df9` covers the GUI session work kind's observe/act interface. The two initiatives converged on a shared transport; see "Shared tunnel" below.

## Decisions

### D1. EFS for `/org` on AWS hosts — `/workspace` is not on EFS (2026-09-07)

> **Scope narrowed twice.** With D2 withdrawn, "mounted by every host class" means **every AWS host**. There is no non-AWS host that mounts EFS: accelerated batch (D8) is object I/O only, and the local interactive host is not viable (`chatticus-9af381` A0, decision `chatticus-e8380b`).
>
> **Measured: D1 fails for `/workspace`.** `chatticus-3d5357` (PR #311): throwaway General Purpose EFS vs local EBS on the same AL2023 instance, same A0 fixture. Mutating A0 `ratio_overall` **23–54×** vs EBS — over the frozen >10× line. Read-only warm `git status` (no mutation, RPC-validated): **~10×** at default/15/60/300 `actimeo` (RPC 203→131, not near-zero); `actimeo=1` thrashes (warm RPC 480, **29×**). The hot working tree is host-local. EFS, if built, is **`/org` only**.
>
> **Do not write product EFS CDK that mounts `/workspace`.** This initiative remains discovery-only. Taking `/workspace` off EFS reopens how that tree moves between hosts (snapshot/hydrate vs `computer_id` pin). That is recorded, not authorized as implementation.

`/org` (durable org files) and `/workspace` (hot working tree) are **not** one EFS filesystem. `/workspace` stays on the host. S3 keeps the jobs it is already good at per `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`: screenshots, artifacts, backups.

This supersedes `docs/COMPUTER_MANIFOLD.md` decisions 2 and 6 as a design *target* only for `/org` on AWS hosts. Those decisions still describe the **live** S3 snapshot workplace until a later implementation epic exists.

### D2. ~~Local hosts mount EFS over an on-demand tunnel~~ — SUPERSEDED 2026-09-07

> **This decision is withdrawn.** `chatticus-9af381` Phase A0 measured 1650x against local disk at ~25 ms RTT — row three of the threshold table agreed in advance. The local interactive host is not viable, and it was the **only remaining consumer of the tunnel**: accelerated batch is object I/O only (D8), and the local-VM display case goes away with the local GUI host. There is no WireGuard peer, no stopped-when-idle EC2 endpoint, no key distribution, and no ~$0.65/mo idle floor, because there is nothing on the far side of the tunnel.
>
> The Fargate finding below stays on the record as verified fact (`chatticus-0b10d6`) — it is simply no longer load-bearing, since there is no tunnel endpoint to place. Decision and cascade: `chatticus-e8380b`.
>
> **What survives:** EFS is a candidate for **`/org` on AWS hosts only** (D1). `/workspace` is not on EFS (`chatticus-3d5357`). Original text kept below for history.

A local worker is **always a Linux (Antharchy) VM**, never macOS directly. That removes the "macOS NFS client is finicky" objection from the earlier draft entirely: the client is a Linux kernel NFSv4.1 client with working `amazon-efs-utils`.

EFS mount targets are VPC-private ENIs on TCP/2049, so a worker outside the VPC needs an IP path in. A **self-hosted WireGuard peer** on a stopped-when-idle EC2 instance provides it:

- WireGuard is open source and kernel-native in the guest. No commercial dependency.
- The endpoint must be EC2. Fargate supports neither privileged mode nor `NET_ADMIN`/`/dev/net/tun`, so it cannot host a WireGuard peer. Verified 2026-09-05 (`chatticus-0b10d6`): ECS Fargate allows only `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` via `linuxParameters.capabilities.add`; `privileged` and `linuxParameters.devices` are unsupported. Live `RegisterTaskDefinition` with `NET_ADMIN` rejected: `ClientException: NET_ADMIN is not allowed on Fargate` (account 335163751677, us-east-1).
- Stopped instance idle cost is its EBS volume only — roughly $0.65/mo for 8 GB gp3. Start latency ~30 s, once per session, amortized across the session.
- The worker already pulls from SQS, so "bring up this org's tunnel endpoint" is an ordinary job, not new machinery.

### D3. ~~There is no lease, and no snapshot protocol~~ — REFUTED 2026-09-07

> **Do not delete the lease or the snapshot protocol. They are load-bearing.**
>
> This decision's whole argument was conditional on `/workspace` living on EFS. `chatticus-3d5357` measured in-VPC EFS at **23–54x mutating** and **~10x read-only warm** against local EBS, so D1 is narrowed to `/org` only and **the hot working tree stays on host-local disk.**
>
> A workspace on host-local disk must still move between hosts for relocate and failover. That is exactly what publish/hydrate is for, and it needs `acquire_computer_disk_write`, `hydrate_required`, and the snapshot manifest. **The snapshot protocol is permanent, not transitional.** `features/computer_snapshots.feature`, `features/computer_snapshot_pack.feature`, and `docs/COMPUTER_SNAPSHOTS.md` describe the shipping design and must not be unwound.
>
> The S3-has-no-locking observation below remains true and is now simply the reason the protocol exists, rather than the reason to remove it. Original text kept below for history.

The lease (`acquire_computer_disk_write` in `python/src/chatticus/computer_start_driver.py`), `hydrate_required`, publish/hydrate, the snapshot manifest, and relocate-as-publish-then-hydrate all exist for exactly one reason: **S3 has no locking.** Two hosts can both hydrate a snapshot, both write, and both publish, and the second publish silently destroys the first. Nothing in S3 prevents it, so coordination has to be bolted on out of band.

EFS is a real filesystem with POSIX locking — `flock`, byte-range locks, concurrent clients. The two-writer problem does not get *solved*; it stops existing, because there is one disk.

**Qualified 2026-09-05.** That holds for **write arbitration**. It does not hold for **cache coherence**: separate NFS clients on different hosts can read stale attributes and directory entries for up to the attribute-cache timeout, which locking does nothing about. Since `chatticus-766c51` established that concurrent turns for one bot are permitted and may land on different hosts, some coordination may return — at the scheduling layer rather than the storage layer, and for a different reason than the S3 lease. See `chatticus-ea918a`.

### D4. Host scratch is not a store

Regenerable output — build directories, `node_modules`, package caches, `/tmp` — lives on host-local disk, never crosses the tunnel, and is never canonical. This is where the WAN write-latency problem goes. It is a tmp directory, not a second tier of storage.

### D5. ~~WAN latency is handled with stock Linux, not architecture~~ — REFUTED 2026-09-07

> **Measured and refuted.** `chatticus-9af381` Phase A0: warm `git status` 32.3 s over ~25 ms RTT versus 0.02 s local — 1650x. `nconnect`, `actimeo` and host scratch did not bring it near the threshold table. The mitigations in this decision do not work at WAN latency, and with D2 withdrawn there is no WAN mount left to mitigate.
>
> **The in-VPC mechanism claim is now measured (`chatticus-3d5357`).** A read-only `git status` loop with no mutation: long `actimeo` cuts RPC only ~35% (203→131), warm wall ~10× EBS, `cache_warm=False`. `actimeo=1` thrashes (warm RPC 480). Long `actimeo` does not make a hot tree viable on EFS. Original text kept below for history.

NFS costs a round trip per `stat`, `open`, and `readdir`; metadata-heavy work (`git status` on a large tree, dependency installs) does tens of thousands of them. Over a home link that is the real cost of D2, and no choice of tunnel changes it.

Mitigations, all boring and off-the-shelf:

- A **long `actimeo`** (`acregmin`/`acregmax`/`acdirmin`/`acdirmax`) holds directory entries and attributes in the client's cache so repeat lookups do not cross the link. This is the load-bearing mitigation.
- `nconnect` for parallel channels. Helps throughput and concurrency; does not reduce per-operation RTT.
- D4 keeps the write-heavy, regenerable traffic off the link entirely.

**Correction, 2026-09-05.** This decision previously named `cachefilesd` / FS-Cache as the mitigation for metadata reads. That is wrong in a way that matters: `fsc` caches file **data pages**, while directory lookups and attributes — essentially all `git status` does, thousands of `lstat` calls — are governed by the **attribute cache**, a different mechanism. FS-Cache is documented as frequently unhelpful and occasionally counterproductive for metadata-heavy work.

The real lever is the attribute cache timeout. The 2026-09-05 correction justified setting it long by appealing to "single-writer-per-workspace scoping recorded below."

**That justification was falsified the same day by `chatticus-766c51`.** Turns are not serialized per bot, and the default is one workspace per bot, so the default configuration has concurrent turns sharing one workspace. A long `actimeo` is therefore **not** established as safe, and D5's load-bearing mitigation is currently unsupported.

Note the failure mode is **staleness, not corruption**: NFS byte-range locking arbitrates writers, and close-to-open consistency does not help because `git status` calls `lstat()` rather than `open()`. Two turns on one NFS client are coherent; the hazard is concurrent turns for one bot placed on **different hosts** sharing a workspace, which the scheduler permits.

**D5 is settled as refuted for a hot tree** (WAN and in-VPC). See `chatticus-ea918a` for `/org` cache coherence under concurrent turns on different hosts — that is not a reason to put `/workspace` back on EFS.

### D6. ~~Tunnel health is worker health~~ — MOOT 2026-09-07

> Withdrawn with D2. With no tunnel there is no tunnel-health signal to fold into the heartbeat. Original text kept below for history.

If the tunnel is down, the local worker's heartbeat goes stale and `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` routing rule 1 already sends the turn to an AWS host. There is no offline mode, no degraded mode, and no new mechanism. The local worker advertises itself only while its mount is live.

This is acceptable **because the local host exists to save money, not to provide sovereignty or offline capability** (see "Why the local host exists").

### D6a. Files versus objects — S3 keeps the objects

EFS is the store for the **filesystem**: `/org`, `/workspace`, the things a
process opens, stats, and walks. **Large artifacts stay objects in S3** — screenshots,
build artifacts, training datasets, model weights, checkpoints. `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`
already routes "object files / artifacts" to S3, so this is not new and not a second
file store; it is the existing files/objects boundary drawn explicitly.

Two forces make it the right line:

- **Cost per GB.** EFS runs roughly an order of magnitude above S3. A multi-hundred-GB
  dataset on EFS is a budget line item; on S3 it is noise.
- **Access shape.** Weights and datasets are written once and read sequentially. That
  is object I/O. Putting them on a POSIX filesystem buys locking and metadata semantics
  they do not use, and pays WAN metadata latency for nothing.

A host doing object-only work therefore needs **no mount and no tunnel** — just SQS and
scoped S3 credentials. See D8.

### D7. Connectivity is a requirement, not a product

No commercial service is named in the architecture. The requirement is: *an outbound-only, authenticated tunnel from host to control plane; the host never accepts inbound connections.* Implementations are an operator deployment choice — WireGuard (default), reverse SSH, SSM Session Manager, or Tailscale/Headscale for convenience. Nothing in the Chatticus codebase imports any of them.

### D8. Accelerated batch is a host class with no storage requirements

**Added 2026-09-03**, after the initial economics below were shown to anchor on the
wrong host class.

ML training, fine-tuning, and long GPU runs are a work kind whose local-host case is
far stronger than interactive work, and whose requirements are far thinner:

- **No display**, so nothing from `chatticus-3c6df9` applies.
- **No filesystem mount**, so nothing from D1–D5 applies. No tunnel, no NFS, no
  FS-Cache, no WAN metadata latency.
- **Object I/O only**: pull or hold the dataset, train, `PUT` the weights to S3.

It needs SQS and scoped S3 credentials as **necessary but not sufficient** surfaces.

**Corrected 2026-09-05 (`chatticus-0edb18`).** Those credentials move artifacts; they do not make a multi-day training run a turn. The turn loop (`turn_deadline` 120 s, recovery exhausted at ~4.5 min), SQS visibility (180 s default, 12 h AWS max), and heartbeat stale-drop (30 s, no busy-vs-dead) all assume short work. Accelerated batch needs a **manifold job kind** (submit / poll / complete) with results as S3 objects, not a stretched turn timeout.

**Free ingress is the asymmetry that makes it work.** Data transfer *into* AWS is free;
egress is ~$0.09/GB. So the cheapest arrangement is also the natural one: keep the
corpus on the side of the boundary where it is consumed, train locally, push weights
in. Egress is only incurred if a local host pulls a large dataset *out* of AWS — which
is an argument about where training data lives, not about this design.

This also reframes what the local-host story is *for*. "My old Mac saves $40/month" is
a weak position. "Plug your own GPU hardware into the manifold and keep the AWS bill for
what actually needs AWS" is a product position — and for organizations with data-residency
or compliance constraints on training corpora, local training is not an optimization at
all but a requirement.

## Scope boundaries

### Workspace becomes a first-class identity

Today the computer is **organization-scoped** (`computer_for_organization` in `computer_start_driver.py`), every bot in an org shares it (`features/single_computer_start.feature`), and the write lease is keyed by **host**, not by bot. So `/workspace` is already org-scoped with no per-bot isolation — `/workspace` and `/org` are currently the same scope under two names. That is the source of the boundary confusion, and it is a real gap rather than a naming problem.

Proposed scopes:

| Scope | Contents | Live writers | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Org** — `/org` | Filing cabinet, shared reference, artifacts of record | many, NFS locks | permanent |
| **Workspace** — `/workspace` | A working tree; attachable, movable between computers | one | until deleted |
| **Bot profile** | Browser profile, cookies, per-bot credentials | one | with the bot |
| **Host scratch** | Build output, caches, `/tmp` | one | with the host; never canonical |

`workspace_id` should be a **first-class noun, not an attribute of the bot.** The decomposition separates agent from compute from storage; scoping storage by the agent re-couples two of the three. A turn declares two independent things: what kind of work (manifold picks a computer) and what data it needs (system attaches a workspace, mounts `/org`). Default is one workspace per bot, so the common case reads as "the bot's files" and the seam is invisible until needed.

### The browser profile must split off from the workspace

`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` bundles `/workspace` and the browser profile into one snapshot. Once a workspace can attach to more than one bot, a bundled profile means **shared cookies across bots** — a cross-bot credential leak. The profile is bot identity; the workspace is files. Different scopes.

### The `computer_id` pin becomes an optimization

`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` pins turns to a `computer_id` because "cookies and `/workspace` stay on one workplace." That pin exists only because storage is host-scoped. Rescope storage and it degrades to "prefer the host that is already warm" — which is what `prefer_local` wanted, and which `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` already flags as misnamed.

## ~~Shared tunnel with the display path~~ — WITHDRAWN 2026-09-07

> The "one tunnel carries both NFS and reverse VNC" argument loses both consumers with D2. `chatticus-3c6df9` keeps **worker-dials-out** as its transport for EC2 Antharchy, which was always the stronger half of that argument and does not depend on this initiative. Original text kept below for history.

`chatticus-3c6df9` independently needs an outbound path for watch/takeover. It is the **same tunnel and the same on-demand endpoint**: one piece of per-org infrastructure, started when a local worker wakes, carrying both NFS and the reverse VNC channel.

The display path also unifies on **worker-dials-out**. `3c6df9`'s v1 (`ssh -L 5900 ... arch@host`) is a human dialing *into* the EC2, which cannot work for a VM behind a home router and contradicts `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` ("the control plane never SSHs into the garage"). Flipping the direction makes one mechanism serve both host classes.

## Why the local host exists — and the budget that follows

The garage Mac exists to **save money on compute** by using hardware that is on anyway. `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` already sets the admission rule: a pool bought *for* Chatticus is an idle floor and is rejected; one that exists anyway has no marginal cost. The garage Mac passes.

Multiplying the numbers out (planning anchors from `docs/COMPUTER_MANIFOLD.md` §5 and `chatticus-3c6df9`; recheck before budgeting):

| Host displaced | Rate | 8 h/day for a month |
|---|---|---|
| Fargate ARM64 0.25 vCPU / 512 MiB | ~$0.01/hr | ~$2.40 |
| t3.xlarge Antharchy GUI session | ~$0.17/hr | ~$41 |

The slim Fargate computer is already nearly free, so displacing it saves pocket change. The savings are real only for the **GUI session class**, in proportion to how many Antharchy VMs the Mac can host — realistically one or two, so $40–80/month. The local path gives back $10–20/month of that in EFS storage, the tunnel endpoint, and NFS egress at ~$0.09/GB on cache misses.

**Net: roughly $30–60/month** for the interactive host class. Any day of design or
implementation spent on *that* case alone costs more than a year of it.

### The GPU case, which changes the budget

**Amended 2026-09-03.** The table above anchors on displacing cheap hosts, and that is
not where owned hardware pays. Accelerated batch (D8) displaces a different tier
entirely:

| Host displaced | Rate | A 40-hour training run |
|---|---|---|
| g5.xlarge (A10G) | ~$1.00/hr | ~$40 |
| p4d.24xlarge (8× A100) | ~$32/hr | ~$1,280 |
| p5.48xlarge (8× H100) | ~$98/hr | ~$3,900 |

*(Recheck before budgeting.)*

An organization training models on hardware it already owns is saving four figures per
run, not tens of dollars per month. And per D8, that host class is the **cheapest one to
support** — no tunnel, no mount, no display.

So the complexity budget is not one number. It splits:

| Host class | Savings | Requirements | Complexity justified |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accelerated batch (GPU, owned) | $100s–$1000s per run | SQS + S3 credentials | High value, near-zero cost — **do this first** |
| GUI session (Antharchy, local) | ~$30–60/mo | Tunnel, EFS mount, FS-Cache, reverse VNC | Thin. Keep it boring. |
| Slim computer (Fargate) | ~$2.40/mo | — | None. Do not bother. |

The ordering is the useful output: the highest-value non-AWS host class is also the
thinnest to build, and it does not depend on any of D1–D5 landing first.

### The reason that survives regardless of the numbers

`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` claims the protocol is substrate-agnostic — adding a host type means adding a cost class and its rank, not changing the architecture. The garage Mac is the only host available that can **falsify** that claim. If the local host needs its own storage system, the claim is false. If it mounts the same EFS and the scheduler simply ranks it cheaper, the claim is proven. That is worth more than the compute dollars, and it argues for the same answer more strongly: the local path must be boring and identical.

## Rejected alternatives

### EFS primary + S3 bridge, split by data shape (the earlier draft) — ~~REJECTED~~ **THIS IS WHAT WON**

> **Reinstated 2026-09-07 by measurement.** This alternative was rejected on the argument that the split was drawn on the wrong axis and that only network topology forced S3. `chatticus-3d5357` showed the axis was right after all: EFS is 23–54x local for a mutating hot tree and ~10x read-only warm, entirely inside one VPC with no WAN involved. Data shape, not network topology, is what separates these stores.
>
> **The shipping design is the data-shape split:** `/workspace` on host-local disk with S3 snapshots for relocate, `/org` on EFS if it is ever built, objects in S3 (D6a). Read the rejection below as the argument that measurement overturned — not as guidance.

Rejected. The split was drawn on the wrong axis. Nothing about a working tree makes it prefer an object store — it wants a filesystem more than `/org` does. The only thing forcing S3 was **network topology** (a worker outside AWS cannot reach a VPC-private mount target), and D2 solves exactly that. The draft proposed a second store to work around a problem it had already solved elsewhere.

### Two-hop sync: local disk ↔ S3 clone ↔ EFS, eventually consistent

Rejected. "Eventually consistent" is safe for a single-writer handoff and dangerous for concurrent writers, and filesystems are the worst case: there is no merge semantics for a directory tree, no CRDT, no three-way merge. rsync, DataSync, and Mutagen all resolve by timestamp, which is **silent data loss**, not a conflict marker.

It would also require building: a lease protocol, an AWS-side S3↔EFS sync engine, a conflict policy at each hop, staleness bounds, and reasoning about how two eventually-consistent legs compose. That is a distributed-systems project, and the complexity budget above does not fund it.

### Tailscale as the connectivity layer

Rejected as an architectural dependency, but **not primarily on "it is commercial" grounds** — that argument does not survive contact:

- Tailscale's client is BSD-licensed, and Headscale is an open-source coordination server. Self-hosting the whole stack is available.
- By the vendor test, **EFS is the more proprietary piece of this design**, not Tailscale.
- Both have open protocols with self-hostable implementations (WireGuard/Headscale; NFSv4.1/Ceph). The vendor axis does not separate them.

The real reason is D7: naming any product in the architecture over-specifies a requirement that several implementations satisfy. WireGuard is chosen as the default because it is the smallest thing that meets the requirement, not because Tailscale is disqualified.

### AWS-managed VPN paths

Rejected on the idle-cost floor. AWS Client VPN is roughly $0.10/hr per subnet association plus $0.05/hr per connection (~$73/mo); Site-to-Site VPN is roughly $0.05/hr (~$36/mo). Both exceed the entire savings the local host produces. Self-hosted WireGuard on a stopped-when-idle instance is ~$0.65/mo. *(Recheck pricing before budgeting.)*

### Mac mounts EFS directly

Moot under the corrected premise: there is no Mac client. The local host is a Linux VM (D2).

## Corrections to the earlier draft

- **"No NAT Gateway needed — Tailscale punches through NAT"** conflates home-router NAT traversal with AWS NAT Gateway, which concerns egress from private subnets and is unaffected either way.
- **"macOS NFS client is finicky"** does not apply; the client is always Linux.
- The **security-model table** listed Tailscale as the network layer protecting EFS access while the same document recommended S3-indirect for local hosts, in which case there was nothing for it to carry.
- The **Taildrop / DHH** passage was product trivia, not architecture.

## Security model

| Layer | Protection |
|---|---|
| Network | WireGuard — mutual key auth, modern crypto, outbound-initiated, no inbound ports on the host |
| Blast radius | Security group permits 2049 to the EFS mount target only. Without this the tunnel grants a general VPC route, which is materially worse than scoped S3 credentials. **This is the control that makes D2 acceptable.** |
| Tenant isolation | EFS access points pin uid/gid and a subdirectory root per org |
| Host isolation | Mount lives inside the Antharchy VM, not on the host OS |
| Revocation | Remove the peer's public key; the route dies immediately |
| Bot isolation | Browser profile scoped per bot, never bundled with a shared workspace |

Note honestly: WireGuard and scoped S3 credentials fail *differently* rather than one being strictly safer. S3 grants no network position at all; WireGuard grants a route into the VPC. Properly scoped, the blast radius collapses to one org's directory — the same as S3's. Unscoped, it is worse. The security-group scoping is load-bearing, not hygiene.

## ~~Migration cost~~ — NO MIGRATION 2026-09-07

> There is nothing to unwind. With D3 refuted, the snapshot path is not a transitional artifact waiting for EFS to replace it — it is the shipping design for `/workspace`. The guidance below ("let EFS arrive as the new mount, allowing the snapshot code to stop being exercised") is **withdrawn**; acting on it would delete working code that the measured design depends on. Original text kept below for history.

The deletion in D3 touches currently-green code and specs: `features/computer_snapshots.feature`, `features/computer_snapshot_pack.feature`, `docs/COMPUTER_SNAPSHOTS.md`, and the snapshot paths in the scheduler.

Given the complexity budget, if unwinding that is more than a few days, the honest sequencing is to **leave the snapshot path in place and let EFS arrive as the new mount**, allowing the snapshot code to stop being exercised rather than ripping it out up front.

## Open questions

### Concurrency and scope

- **Can one bot have two turns in flight at once?** **Yes — answered 2026-09-05 (chatticus-766c51).** The control plane does not serialize turns per bot. ``enqueue_turn`` and ``_start_turn_for_bot`` create a new turn and job with no check for an existing active turn or pending job on that ``bot_id``. ``pending_jobs_for_bot`` returns all queued jobs; workers may drain several per bot via ``complete_pending_for_bot``.

  **Evidence:** ``features/messages.feature`` lists two active turns for one bot on two channels. A read-only probe confirms the same channel allows two ACTIVE turns with two pending jobs; the durable active-turn pointer is per-channel and shows only the latest, so an older concurrent turn on the same channel remains ACTIVE but is omitted from ``get_active_turn`` / ``list_active_turns`` for that channel.

  **Not the same as turn-attempt dedup:** ``features/turn_attempts.feature`` fences duplicate *delivery* of one logical enqueue for a single ``turn_id`` (``claim_turn_attempt``, ``logical_enqueue_id(turn_id)``). That prevents one request becoming two answers; it does not limit one bot to one turn.

  **Routine wake-up:** Routines are not fully implemented in production code; the CLI path ``find_or_open_channel`` reuses the first channel that already includes the bot or opens a new one. Either way, nothing blocks a second turn while the first is live.

  **Scoping consequence — ``workspace_id``:** Default one workspace per bot is a convenience default, not a concurrency guarantee. Concurrent turns on the same bot must not assume an exclusive working tree unless each turn declares its own ``workspace_id``. ``/workspace`` is **not** on EFS (`chatticus-3d5357`), so NFS attribute-cache staleness does not apply to the hot tree. ``workspace_id`` is the product isolation boundary, not an NFS coherence lever. Remaining EFS (``/org``) still has a default-``actimeo`` staleness window across hosts; that is ``chatticus-ea918a``.

  **Scoping consequence — ``hydrate_required``:** This gate is **computer/org-scoped**, not bot-scoped. During the snapshot-to-EFS transition it pins ``assign_turn`` to the intended host until ``hydrate_computer`` completes; concurrent computer-capable turns on the same household computer queue behind the same hydrate pin and org-level host-start / disk-write lease (``features/single_computer_start.feature``). It is not a bot turn mutex; it disappears once EFS replaces the snapshot hydrate path (D3).
- Does `/org` need its own write coordination above NFS locks, or is POSIX locking sufficient for the filing-cabinet access pattern?
- Migration path for existing org-scoped `/workspace` content into the new scopes.

### ~~Tunnel~~ — CLOSED 2026-09-07 (no tunnel)

> All questions in this section are moot with D2 withdrawn: no endpoint to own, no start latency to gate on, no keys to rotate. The Fargate capability question was answered anyway (`chatticus-0b10d6`) and stays true. Original text kept below for history.


- Who owns the endpoint's lifecycle — the manifold, or a separate per-org connectivity resource?
- Endpoint start latency (~30 s) versus the turn's readiness gates in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`: which gate does the mount block?
- Key distribution and rotation for the WireGuard peers.

### Accelerated batch (D8)

- Does it belong in this initiative or its own? It shares the "non-AWS compute" premise
  but none of the storage mechanism.
- How does a worker advertise GPU capability, and how does the manifold rank owned
  hardware against g5/p4d/p5?
- Where do training corpora live by default, given free ingress and charged egress?
- Long-running jobs versus the 120 s worker poll ceiling in `docs/COMPUTER_MANIFOLD.md`
  — a multi-day training run is the extreme case of the headless-session problem.
- Weight files as objects: versioning, naming, and whether they are org-scoped artifacts
  or workspace contents.

### Measurement (should precede implementation)

- ~~Real `git status` over a tunnel~~ — closed with D2 / A0 WAN (1650×) and `chatticus-3d5357` in-VPC (mutating 23–54× vs EBS; read-only ~10×). `/workspace` is not on EFS.
- EFS storage cost per org at realistic **`/org`** sizes, if `/org`-only EFS is ever implemented.

### Databases (unchanged from the earlier draft, still open)

- Relational (RDS) or document (DynamoDB) per organization; which is the default given RDS has an idle floor and DynamoDB is pay-per-request?
- When is an org's database provisioned — at org creation, or on first request?
- Local workers reach it through the same tunnel as NFS and VNC; the agent sees a connection string and does not know whether access is direct or tunneled.

comments.text:
## D8 correction (spike chatticus-0edb18, 2026-09-05)

**Corrected:** D8 stated accelerated batch needs only SQS and scoped S3 credentials — "That is the entire integration."

The long-job spike shows those surfaces are **necessary but not sufficient** when work is modeled as a turn:

- SQS + S3 can move artifacts, but the turn loop fails long before batch work finishes (`turn_deadline` 120 s, recovery exhausted at ~4.5 min on the 30 min authorized run).
- SQS visibility (180 s default, 12 h max) and missing renew on the computer pull path cannot carry multi-day jobs.
- Heartbeat timeout (30 s) drops busy workers unless separately heartbeating.

**Revised claim:** An accelerated-batch host needs SQS and scoped S3 credentials **plus a non-turn job kind** in the manifold (submit / poll / complete), with results as S3 objects rather than streamed turn output.

Evidence: PR #307, `spikes/long-running-job-0edb18/results/final/`.

comments.text:
## Learnings from `e9ddec` (2026-09-05)

Live AWS + code reading. Design conclusions, not implementation.

1. **D2 verified.** Tunnel endpoint stays stopped-when-idle EC2. Fargate cannot add `NET_ADMIN` or map `/dev/net/tun`. Scale-to-zero tunnel is not available. Idle-floor math (~\$0.65/mo EBS) stands.

2. **D8 corrected.** "SQS + scoped S3 is the entire integration" is false for work modeled as a turn. Those surfaces move artifacts. They do not carry multi-day jobs: `turn_deadline` 120 s, recovery exhausted ~4.5 min, SQS visibility 180 s (12 h AWS max), heartbeat 30 s with no busy-vs-dead. Accelerated batch needs a **job kind** (submit / poll / complete) with S3 objects as results.

3. **Concurrency answered; D5 not settled.** One bot may have many in-flight turns. Default one workspace per bot is not a lock. Long `actimeo` was justified as safe only under single-writer-per-workspace; `766c51` shows the default configuration does not provide that when concurrent turns share a bot workspace across hosts. Failure mode is staleness (`lstat` / `git status`), not NFS write corruption. Decision: `chatticus-ea918a`. `hydrate_required` is computer/org-scoped until D3 deletes the snapshot path.

4. **D5 still unmeasured.** FS-Cache vs attribute-cache correction is in D5. NFS-over-WAN numbers cannot be taken until CDK creates a Chatticus workplace EFS and tunnel. Phase A0 (netem, `9af381`) can still answer whether any threshold-table row is reachable in principle, without AWS.

EFS-for-AWS-hosts does not wait on the WAN spike. Accelerated batch does not wait on EFS. Local interactive host does. Cache-coherence under concurrent turns is a design question on the AWS-host track too (`ea918a`).

comments.text:
## D3 correction — do not delete the snapshot protocol (2026-09-07)

Flagging this because `3d5357` closing changed D3's status and the issue text had not caught up. It is the one leftover that could cost working code.

D3 ("there is no lease, and no snapshot protocol") argued the lease, `hydrate_required`, publish/hydrate and the manifest exist **only** because S3 lacks locking, and that EFS's POSIX locking retires them. That argument was entirely conditional on `/workspace` living on EFS.

It does not. `/workspace` stays on host-local disk, and a workspace on host-local disk still has to move between hosts for relocate and failover — which is exactly what publish/hydrate does. **The snapshot protocol is permanent, not transitional.**

Corrected in the description: D3 struck through and marked refuted; the "Migration cost" section withdrawn, since its guidance was to let the snapshot code stop being exercised as EFS took over. `features/computer_snapshots.feature`, `features/computer_snapshot_pack.feature`, `docs/COMPUTER_SNAPSHOTS.md` and the scheduler snapshot paths all describe the shipping design and stay.

Also corrected: **"EFS primary + S3 bridge, split by data shape" is listed under Rejected alternatives and is what won.** `3d5357` measured 23–54x entirely inside one VPC with no WAN involved, so the axis was data shape, not network topology. Left in place with the rejection struck through, since the argument measurement overturned is worth keeping visible.

A terminal outcome summary is now at the top of the description.

comments.author: home
comments.text:
## Ordering caveat found 2026-09-07 — not a reopening

This initiative spent three days deciding **where `/workspace` should live**. It has since emerged that **no agent-facing tool can reach the container's `/workspace` at all.**

Two file layers ship and are not connected:

- `ControlPlane.read_workspace` / `write_workspace` → an **in-process dict** (`computer.workspace`), which `put_computer` does not persist, so a ThinTurn recycle starts empty. This is what agent tools reach.
- `chatticus.snapshot` (`pack_live_disk` / `unpack_live_disk`) → **real directories**, exactly as `COMPUTER_SNAPSHOTS.md` specifies. Tested, exercised by `python -m chatticus.snapshot`, and called by **no production path** — the Fargate host worker never publishes or hydrates. Verified: the only references are the module's own exports and `python/tests/test_snapshot_pack.py`.

`publish_snapshot` bridges them for Gherkin only, by copying the dict.

**Nothing here is invalidated.** The `chatticus-3d5357` measurements are real, EFS is still measured out, and the data-shape split still stands. But the order was inverted: we answered *where workspace files should live* before establishing *whether agents can use workspace files at all*. The answer to the second is currently no.

**One correction to a claim this initiative produced.** `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` was edited on 2026-09-07 to call the snapshot protocol "the shipping design". That overstated it — the library is real and tested but unwired. Corrected in the same doc: it is the **design target**, "do not delete" still holds, but it is not load-bearing in production today.

**The live decision is on `chatticus-3e72dc`:** leave agent files as the dict, or wire the tools to host disk (and then `chatticus-bb9084`'s bucket). That decision, not this initiative, determines whether any of the storage reasoning here becomes operative.

comments.text: Operative-vs-aspirational (2026-09-07): D3 / host-local `/workspace` + S3 snapshots remain the **design target** (`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` `4142832`, not the earlier "shipping design" wording). They are only *operative* if agent file tools are wired to host disk (`chatticus-fccc4e9a-b3c6-4a14-9317-d0b0c95231b7`). Under the dict branch this initiative's conclusions stay true as a target and the snapshot library still must not be deleted, but no agent writes the trees the library packs. Storage discovery stays closed: no `/workspace` EFS, no tunnel.
